title: have several games underway but I cant stick to developing one?
author: retrorays
selftext:
This might be a me thing, but I have several games I'm developing. At a certain point when I work on one I lose inspiration, and then jump to another game. Make some progress... get a bit bummed out about it and then back to the previous game. 

Is this a typical thing with gamedev and AI development in particular?  It's like - wow I can do this, look how cool it is, then you get disappointed/bored, and move to something else. Then later I get more inspiration on the previous game and come back. 

In all cases I feel like the game is never ready. At least not where I really want to play it extensively myself.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
you don't have to stick to developing one unless you want to ship one of them quickly. 

if you are a solo dev, there is no schedule so do whatever you want.

replies.author: retrorays
replies.body: thanks - yah solo w/ my AI "buddies". Always wanted to develop games in my part time but never had time. Now w/ AI time is less of an issue. Ironically I find creativity is my issue. I have immense respect for those that make games now that I've gone through several part-way. It's crazy hard to make them innovative **and** fun.

comments.author: -Star-Walker-
comments.body: Even in ai development, the Pareto principle is present. Do the first 80% of your work in 20% of the time needed, spend another 80% of the time on the remaining 20% of work. That’s balancing, fine-tuning, bug fixing, … all things where you barely see any progress.

comments.author: TheUniverseOrNothing
comments.body:
I have the same issue but honestly I enjoy having more than one project. I’m in no rush to finish them and when I need to spend some time just doing play testing one game I can have the other being worked on.

I started a new discord with other builders and that’s really been helping me stay on track. I share certain features I like and still get feedback without having pressure of releasing full game.

comments.author: EnumeratedArray
comments.body:
This is incredibly common. I think AI just makes it feel worse since you can have more projects in flight at once.

If it's getting you down, start massively reducing your scope, and focus on finishing something rather than building a specific game. Finish something simple, just for yourself, like a Tetris clone, sudoku game, etc.

replies.author: retrorays
replies.body: architecting and defining the game foundation. Identifying assets, maybe building myself, maybe using AI. Then developing w/ AI agents for foundational code, features etc.  Iteration takes days to weeks before real development starts. Then development is iterative, validate, vibe, code, repeat for each stage until something seems acceptable.

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body: Maybe you need to be patient until one is good enough to pull you in fully? I spent the last month experimenting. One game, then 2, 3, 6 more prototypes I scrapped, back to working on 3, then only two were showing progress, and finally I hit dome breakthroughs on one of them and it completely sucked me in and it’s basically all I can think about anymore. Every commit leads to 5 more ideas and it’s just all so fun. The cost of extermination is very cheap eith AI so you can experiment until you find something worth fully committing to.

replies.author: retrorays
replies.body: great point - I actually resurrected one of my old projects from last year. I stopped it because the AI tools couldn't take me much further. The latest tools broke through the roadblocks, and I'm pushing on it to see whether I can get it to my vision of a playable, fun, strategic game.

comments.author: No-Possibility1721
comments.body:
My only advice is to focus on one thing at a time. Treat every project like it's your baby. Nothing is ever truly finished, as every detail can always be tweaked.

So, just stick to one project at a time, and when it’s done, let it go. Don't look back; just start something new and repeat the process. And when it comes to games, I’d suggest learning to build a few things yourself without using AI.

comments.author: Reasonable-Reason901
comments.body:
I’ve had the same experience. I’ve started and stopped at least 8 different games now over the last year. Some of them I spent weeks and months on. My issue is usually poor management of scope where I get so many ideas and AI makes it possible to just keep adding on. So instead of committing to the original vision it always gets morphed into something completely different and loses its identity. 

The best advice I think when you struggle with this problem is to build systems, not games. So that when you eventually abandon something, your time and effort carries over to your next project in some way that makes it all worth it. Whether it’s some sort of library, Claude skill, some design principle or best practice you learn. Make sure whatever workflow you’re using is always improving so even if you ship nothing your next project will always be better. 

In my case I eventually took 2 of my failed games and ended up stealing ideas from each to combine into the game I’ve been working on now for about a week. It’s by far my best project and the first time I’ve ever actually felt good enough about something to post on this sub.

So just keep going and try not to get discouraged when one project doesn’t work out. Also if you have a genuinely good idea that you just don’t execute right, when models get better you can always go back and revisit later, like look at all of the cool shit we’re getting now with opus 5.5. Some of your earlier ideas might have been gold and the models at the time just weren’t the right fit.

comments.author: PeaFar698
comments.body:
I have this issue, kind of, but I’m blocked by the lack of my artistic talent lol. I can nail down mechanics and gray box stuff but art is where I struggle so I just abandon stuff to try and reduce scope and make something much smaller, only to keep doing that until I realize I can’t draw for shit lol. I’ve purchased probably $400 worth of assets and I just kind of have a pile of disparate assets now that I’m not sure what to do with lol. 

So I feel your pain.

replies.author: retrorays
replies.body: yah same - I have some skills, but I'm impatient and slow building anything. The new models can use blender and build assets for you - which is a godsend. They can also make sure the assets have cohesiveness across the map. Also can use those AI modeling sites that will create assets.

replies.author: PeaFar698
replies.body: I didn't even see this sub was AI game dev haha. I would do that, but I get very nervous about doing so since you have to disclose if your game uses generative AI, and that turns off a lot of people who would potentially play your game,

replies.author: retrorays
replies.body: lol - every single game made today uses generative AI. So I wouldnt worry about disclosing it - at all.

comments.author: Frequent-Motor-492
comments.body: You probably don't lose interest. You probably hit the hard work part. That feeling is very good at tricking you into thinking it's something else. Games are a ton of work. Pick your favorite and get building.

comments.author: InformationTop5376
comments.body: For me, I up until recently was focused on several different games at a time. When I really got some positive playtester feedback on one of them, I decided to go full steam ahead (pun intended), and target a steam launch for it next year. I have been planning it out from a wishlist maximization timeline. So looks like it’s gonna be a June or October 2027 release, but I’m working on buying into my steam store page with a coming soon right now to start the process. Even if the game ends up totally sucking, I’m having a blast learning about all the ins and outs of game development, including the marketing angle.
